facts: Anne Thorndike, a primary care physician at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, ran a six-month study in the hospital cafeteria.

The refrigerators next to the cash registers held only soda; her team added water to them and placed baskets of bottled water next to food stations around the room. Soda stayed in the main refrigerators.
Nobody said a word to the people eating there.
Over the next three months soda sales fell 11.4% and bottled water sales rose 25.8%. Similar changes to the food produced similar results.

Context: the published study (Thorndike et al., 2012) first added color-coded traffic-light labels; the water figures come from the later placement phase. A follow-up found the shift toward healthier purchases held for 24 months.
Clear's point: people often choose products for where they are, not what they are; environment is the invisible hand that shapes behaviour.

His suggestions: put pill bottles next to the bathroom faucet; fill a few water bottles and set them around the house. Cookies on the counter get eaten without hunger; vitamins in the pantry are easy to skip.
Clear cites psychologist Kurt Lewin's 1936 equation: behaviour is a function of the person in their environment.

Clear tells of a Dutch suburb in the 1970s energy crisis: nearly identical houses, some with the electric meter in the basement, others in the main upstairs hallway; households that could see their meter used less energy. The exact percentage is left out (not verified).
The chapter is titled 'Motivation Is Overrated; Environment Often Matters More'.
